$schema-note: Hand-maintained. Data, not code: nothing in domain/, application/ or contracts/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for @platos/context-conversations. One entry per
authorization check, scope check, cap, kill switch, step ceiling, abort path
and erasure step in the package, each carrying the file it lives in, the
EXACT text that implements it (`from`), the edit that removes it (`to`), the
suites that are supposed to notice (`suites`), and the named cases that
actually went red when it was removed (`killedBy`).
A guard nothing can turn red is a guard that is not there. All 89 entries
below were exercised before this context was proposed and all 89 were
falsifiable. A guard added later belongs here; one that is not here has not
been shown to be more than a comment.
This lives here rather than in README.md because that file is emitted by
PLACEHOLDERS, never its scaffolding, so an adopted context still owes the
procedure: For one entry: replace its `from` with its `to` in the named file, run
`pnpm exec vitest run <suites>`, and confirm a NAMED case goes red. Then
revert and confirm green. A mutation that leaves every case green is a
finding, not a pass.
No `from` here was transcribed by hand. Each was extracted from the file by
a unique anchor line and its span, and the extractor refuses an anchor that
matches no line or more than one, so a `from` that has drifted from the
source cannot sit in this file looking plausible.
THREE ENTRIES WERE NOT FALSIFIABLE WHEN FIRST WRITTEN, and they are the
reason this file is worth keeping.
M60 (the compaction lock) shared CONVERSATIONS_COMPACTION_IN_PROGRESS with
`beginCompaction`. Two guards on one code cannot be told apart: deleting the
repository's lock check left the domain check answering the identical
refusal and every case stayed green. The race now has its own code,
CONVERSATIONS_COMPACTION_LOCK_HELD, and the suite asserts which of the two
fired.
M62 (releasing the lock when there is nothing to compact) was unfalsifiable
as a transform, and the finding stands rather than being papered over:
`acquireCompactionLock` refuses a row that already says IN_PROGRESS, so the
row the empty-plan path holds is provably IDLE and `releaseCompaction`
cannot change it. THE RELEASE IS THE WRITE, so the mutation removes the
write, which is the thing that would actually strand the lock.
M83 (the target-name check inside `carryOutPlan`) was unreachable through
the published binder, because `erase` rejects any plan its WeakMap does not
know first. It is reachable by a caller that tampers with a plan it did
legitimately obtain — the plan is a plain object — and the suite now does
exactly that.
ONE ENTRY MUTATES A DOUBLE RATHER THAN A USE CASE. M86 removes the cascade
from `deleteThreadsForEndUser` in the in-memory erasure store. `Turn` and
`Step` hang off `Thread` with onDelete: Cascade, and a double that did not
model it would let the erasure suite certify that a subject's own words
outlive the thread that held them.
